name: Expressive maximalism
philosophy: Create abundant visual energy around a stable information spine. The audience can enjoy complexity because the next useful action stays clear.
influences: Poster composition, collage, illustration and expressive editorial work suggest techniques. Memphis is a related visual reference, not a synonym for all maximalism.
characteristics: Multiple saturated color fields with disciplined contrast
Intentional shifts in scale and rhythm
Layered decorative material separated from functional content
typography: A display face can bend the tone, but schedule times and ticket controls need a stable text system. Keep experimental typography to short strings. Use real text rather than images of every headline.
color: Use several hues with explicit surface/text pairings. Define each section as a legible color pair instead of scattering independent random colors. Gradients and glows are valid if they support the world and don't obscure reading.
spacing: High density does not mean all gaps are small. Keep generous breathing room around the primary action and navigation, then pack optional expressive details into controlled fields.
composition: Choose one persistent navigation grammar and one main reading path. Layer the art on separate noninteractive planes. Vary section composition by content type: lineup, schedule, venue, access information.
imagery: Original illustration, performer photography or licensed mixed media should belong to a coherent world. Decorative SVG shapes can support typography without pretending to be real performers or venue imagery.
iconography: An expressive set is welcome; maintain recognizable functional symbols and label unusual controls. Reuse line weight or silhouette logic.
components: Bold ticket controls and vivid selected states. A quiet accessible schedule can coexist with exuberant surrounding art. Do not make every item a competing primary action.
interaction: Program filters preserve event information, visibly identify selected options and announce result counts. Critical information should not depend on hover or a playful discovery gesture.
motion: Choose one dominant rhythm. Avoid stacking parallax, marquee, auto video and scroll hijacking. Offer pause for ongoing content and replace spatial motion in reduced-motion mode.
mobile: Remove secondary decorative overlaps, preserve the lineup order and keep ticket/access information near the top. Test long artist names, translated labels and touch navigation.
accessibility: Test contrast per section and focused state; color cannot be the only schedule category signal. Avoid flashing content and obstructing reading with animation.
mistakes: Changing navigation conventions in each section
Glowing text on equally bright backgrounds
amateurish: Unrelated fonts, random stickers and continuous movement compete with the actual event information.
exceptional: The page is visually abundant yet the visitor can still find date, venue, program and access details immediately.
implementation: Use section-scoped color variables, isolated decorative layers with pointer-events:none, fluid display type and a plain semantic schedule. See the original festival example.
libraries: CSS and SVG for a static visual world; Motion or GSAP only for a demonstrated choreography need. Keep essential content outside canvas/WebGL.
evaluation: Can someone find date, location and action without exploring?
Does every section have a readable foreground/background pair?
Is the static version still expressive and complete?
evidence: Original design recipe; source-linked engineering constraints. Not a validated causal model of visual quality.
